terms.grammar: phrase: perītus with the ablative ūsū
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.147: doctōs hominēs vel ūsū perītōs (Lewis & Short, s.v. perītus)
terms.comment: Ūsus is practice and experience, as against learning (doctrīna); ūsū discere is to learn by doing.
Of things: useful in daily life, as against what is only theory.
A philosophers’ and rhetoricians’ term (Seneca, Quintilian); it is not used of an energetic person (see active).
The Greek πρακτικός in one late author; Seneca and Quintilian say āctīvus.

phrases.latin: philosophia et contemplātīva est et āctīva; spectat simul agitque
phrases.english: philosophy is both theoretical and practical: it looks and at the same time acts

phrases.latin: Hoc ūsū magis quam librīs didicit.
phrases.english: He learnt this by doing it rather than from books.

practicus-a.html: The quantity of the first a is not settled: Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked, and the Greek πρᾱκτικός would make it long. Left unmarked.
